summary: Our familiar companion is a member of Felidae. Domestic cats vary enormously in coat colour, pattern and length; tabbies, Siamese and other breeds belong to the same species.
range: Worldwide, associated with people
habitat: Homes, settlements, farms and feral populations in many environments
identification: Highly variable coat colours and patterns
Size and hair length vary among breeds
Tabby markings can closely resemble wildcats
taxonomy_note: A species match does not identify a breed. Appearance alone cannot reliably separate domestic–wildcat hybrids.

summary: A powerful, social big cat. Lions live in groups called prides, and adult males commonly develop a mane whose appearance varies with age and environment.
range: Parts of sub-Saharan Africa and western India
habitat: Savannas, open woodlands and scrub
identification: Mostly plain tawny coat
Tail ending in a dark tuft
Adult males usually have a mane

summary: A large, striped Asian cat that usually hunts alone. Each animal has its own stripe pattern, which helps break up its outline among vegetation.
range: Fragmented populations across South, Southeast and eastern Asia
habitat: Forests, grasslands and wetlands with cover and prey
identification: Dark vertical stripes
Orange coat with pale underparts in typical individuals
Broad head and powerful build
taxonomy_note: White tigers are a colour variant, not a separate species.

summary: An adaptable big cat found in a wide variety of landscapes. Its spotted coat varies across its range; black individuals are the same species, with markings often still visible.
range: Parts of Africa and Asia
habitat: Forests, savannas, scrub and rocky mountains
identification: Small dark rosettes, usually without central spots
Long tail
Relatively slender build compared with a jaguar
taxonomy_note: A black panther may be a melanistic leopard or jaguar; the term is not a species name.

summary: The largest cat native to the Americas. Jaguars have a robust head and body, and inhabit forests as well as wetlands and other covered landscapes.
range: Mexico through Central America into South America
habitat: Tropical forests, wetlands, wooded savannas and scrub
identification: Large rosettes often containing small spots
Broad head and stocky body
Relatively short tail for a big cat
taxonomy_note: Black individuals are melanistic jaguars, not a separate species.

summary: A mountain specialist adapted to cold, rugged terrain. A thick coat, broad paws and a long, bushy tail help it move and rest in harsh conditions.
range: High mountains of Central and South Asia
habitat: Rocky alpine and subalpine mountains
identification: Pale grey coat with dark rosettes
Exceptionally long, thick tail
Small rounded ears and broad paws

summary: A forest cat with large, irregular coat markings and strong climbing abilities. Its long tail helps it balance in trees.
range: Himalayan foothills and mainland Southeast Asia
habitat: Primarily dense tropical and subtropical forests
identification: Large cloud-shaped dark markings
Long tail approaching body length
Short, sturdy legs and broad paws
taxonomy_note: Separated from the Sunda clouded leopard; a photograph alone may not resolve the two.

summary: A forest-dwelling cat of Borneo and Sumatra. It is closely related to the mainland clouded leopard but recognised as a distinct species.
range: Borneo and Sumatra
habitat: Lowland, hill and montane forests, including some logged forest
identification: Cloud-shaped markings, often smaller than in the mainland species
Grey-toned coat in typical individuals
Long tail and short legs
taxonomy_note: Visual separation from the mainland clouded leopard can be uncertain without origin information.

summary: A lightly built cat specialised for rapid pursuit. Its long limbs and slender body distinguish it from the more powerfully built spotted big cats.
range: Parts of Africa and a remnant population in Iran
habitat: Open grasslands, savannas, shrublands and arid landscapes
identification: Dark tear lines from eyes toward mouth
Small solid spots in the typical coat
Slender body with long legs
taxonomy_note: The king cheetah pattern is a coat variation, not a separate species.

summary: Also called the cougar or mountain lion, this adaptable American cat occupies an exceptionally broad range of habitats. Adults generally have a plain coat; cubs are spotted.
range: Western North America, parts of eastern North America, Central and South America
habitat: Forests, mountains, grasslands, scrub and deserts
identification: Plain tawny or grey-brown adult coat
Long tail with a dark tip
Small rounded ears and powerful hindquarters

summary: An elongated, low-slung cat closely related to the puma. Different individuals may be reddish, grey or dark brown, without the strong spotting of many other American cats.
range: Mexico, Central America and much of South America
habitat: Scrub, woodland, forests, grasslands and wetland edges
identification: Long body and short legs
Small head with rounded ears
Mostly plain coat and long tail
taxonomy_note: Older sources may use Puma yagouaroundi.

summary: An agile cat of often dry, open landscapes. Its tall ears carry conspicuous black tufts, although it is not a member of the lynx genus.
range: Parts of Africa, the Middle East and South Asia
habitat: Savannas, scrub, semi-deserts and open woodland
identification: Long black ear tufts
Plain reddish or sandy coat
Long legs and a relatively short tail

summary: A compact forest cat closely related to the caracal and serval. Despite its name, the coat may be grey or reddish, with variable spotting.
range: Forested parts of West and Central Africa
habitat: Moist tropical forests, including some secondary and montane forest
identification: Rounded ears without long tufts
Compact body and relatively short tail
Grey or reddish coat, sometimes spotted
taxonomy_note: The name Caracal aurata follows the 2017 reference; some newer checklists use Caracal auratus.

summary: A long-legged African cat adapted to finding small prey in grass. Its exceptionally large ears help detect movement in dense vegetation.
range: Mainly sub-Saharan Africa, with a limited northern African presence
habitat: Grasslands, reed beds, marshes and other habitats near water
identification: Very large upright ears
Long legs and a small head
Spotted coat with a short tail

summary: A forest cat with striking variation in colour: golden, grey, dark and patterned individuals occur. Facial stripes are more consistent than its coat colour.
range: Himalayan foothills through Southeast Asia, including Sumatra
habitat: Tropical, subtropical and montane forests
identification: Pale facial lines bordered with dark markings
Rounded ears
Often plain golden-brown coat, but many colour forms occur

summary: A little-studied cat found only on Borneo. It is associated with forest and has a notably long tail; reddish and grey individuals are known.
range: Borneo
habitat: Lowland and hill forests, including some logged forest
identification: Long tail with a pale underside
Small rounded ears
Usually chestnut or grey coat

summary: A small Asian forest cat with an intricate blotched coat. Its very long tail and climbing adaptations suit life among trees.
range: Himalayan foothills through Southeast Asia, Sumatra and Borneo
habitat: Moist tropical and subtropical forests
identification: Irregular marbled blotches outlined in dark fur
Very long, bushy tail
Rounded head and relatively small body

summary: A thick-coated cat of rocky Andean and Patagonian landscapes. It can resemble the pampas cat, making careful comparison necessary.
range: Andean regions of Peru, Bolivia, Chile and Argentina, extending into northern Patagonia
habitat: Rocky, sparsely vegetated mountain and steppe landscapes
identification: Long, thick tail with broad dark rings
Silvery-grey coat with darker blotches
Dark nose in typical individuals

summary: A medium-sized American cat most often associated with dense cover. Its coat carries elongated markings that can join into bands along the sides.
range: Southern North America, Central America and South America
habitat: Forests, thorn scrub, mangroves and other dense vegetation
identification: Elongated rosettes and dark flank bands
Sturdy legs with large paws
Shorter tail than the similar margay

summary: A small, highly skilled climbing cat of American forests. Its large eyes and long tail help distinguish it from the larger ocelot.
range: Mexico through Central America into South America
habitat: Tropical and subtropical forests
identification: Very large eyes
Long, thick tail marked with rings
Rosetted coat and large paws

summary: A variable South American cat represented here by the broad 2017 species concept. Coat colour and markings differ substantially between populations.
range: Western and southern South America under the 2017 broad species concept
habitat: Grasslands, scrub, highland steppe and other open habitats
identification: Broad face and often long fur
Relatively short tail
Leg bars and a pinkish nose in typical individuals
taxonomy_note: This is the broad CCTF 2017 concept. Later treatments split it into several species; this app does not distinguish those splits.

summary: A small spotted cat represented here by the broad northern tiger-cat concept used in 2017. Several populations have since been proposed or recognised as distinct species.
range: Parts of Central and South America under the 2017 broad species concept
habitat: Forests, wooded savannas and scrub, varying by population
identification: Small, slender body
Dark rosettes on a pale to ochre coat
Strong visual overlap with other tiger cats
taxonomy_note: The 2017 concept predates later tiger-cat splits, including clouded tiger cat and the 2026 description of Leopardus tilcayo. This app cannot resolve those taxa.

summary: A small South American cat closely resembling other tiger cats. It occupies forest and some more open habitats, and can be difficult to identify from a single photograph.
range: Southern and southeastern Brazil, Paraguay and northeastern Argentina
habitat: Atlantic Forest, other woodlands and some savannas
identification: Small body with a spotted or rosetted coat
Rosettes often have thick, continuous outlines
Yellow-brown to ochre background colour
taxonomy_note: Similar tiger-cat species may require geographic and genetic evidence for reliable identification.

summary: A small cat of southern South America that uses diverse habitats. Its coat is usually covered in small solid spots; dark individuals also occur.
range: Southern South America, including Bolivia, Brazil, Paraguay, Uruguay, Argentina and Chile
habitat: Grasslands, scrub, woodland and wetlands
identification: Small solid spots rather than large rosettes
Dark cheek stripes
Relatively short, ringed tail

summary: Also known as the guiña, this very small South American cat depends strongly on vegetation cover. It inhabits forests and some surrounding modified landscapes.
range: Central and southern Chile and adjoining Argentina
habitat: Temperate forests, wooded scrub and forest mosaics
identification: Small face and rounded ears
Dense small dark spots
Thick, ringed tail

summary: An adaptable North American cat with a short tail. It resembles the Canada lynx but generally has smaller paws and shorter ear tufts.
range: Southern Canada, the United States and Mexico
habitat: Woodlands, scrub, deserts, wetlands and mixed landscapes
identification: Short tail with a pale underside near the tip
Short ear tufts
Spotted or streaked coat and relatively compact build

summary: A northern forest cat strongly associated with snowshoe hares. Large, densely furred feet help it travel over soft snow.
range: Canada, Alaska and parts of the northern contiguous United States
habitat: Boreal and mixed forests
identification: Very large, furred paws
Long ear tufts and cheek ruff
Short tail with an all-dark tip

summary: The largest lynx species, with long legs and a coat that varies from almost plain to distinctly spotted. It occupies forests and some more open Asian landscapes.
range: Parts of Europe and northern, central and eastern Asia
habitat: Temperate and boreal forests, mountains and some wooded steppe
identification: Long black ear tufts
Short black-tipped tail
Long legs and often a spotted coat

summary: A lynx native to the Iberian Peninsula and strongly dependent on rabbits. Its prominent facial ruff and spotted coat are useful features to compare.
range: Spain and Portugal
habitat: Mediterranean scrub and woodland mosaics
identification: Prominent cheek ruff in adults
Distinct dark spots
Tufted ears and short black-tipped tail

summary: Also called the manul, this thick-coated cat is adapted to cold, dry country. Its flattened face and low-set ears give it a distinctive outline.
range: Central Asia and adjoining mountain and steppe regions
habitat: Rocky steppe, montane grassland and semi-desert
identification: Broad, flattened face
Small rounded ears set low on the head
Dense fur and a thick, ringed tail

summary: One of the smallest cats, this species has a pale coat marked with rusty spots. Dense cover and rocky features are common in its habitats.
range: India, Sri Lanka and parts of Nepal
habitat: Forests, scrub, grassland and rocky areas
identification: Very small body
Rusty-brown spots on a greyish coat
Dark facial stripes and large eyes
taxonomy_note: The correct epithet is rubiginosus; some online indexes contain spelling errors.

summary: A small wetland specialist with an unusually low forehead. Its anatomy is adapted to taking aquatic prey, and it is closely associated with water.
range: Malay Peninsula, Sumatra and Borneo
habitat: Lowland riverine forest, swamp forest and wetlands
identification: Long, narrow head with a flattened forehead
Small low-set ears
Short tail and reddish-brown coat

summary: A sturdy cat often associated with wetlands and fish prey. It is larger and more heavily built than the similar-looking leopard cats.
range: Patchy populations in South and Southeast Asia
habitat: Marshes, mangroves, river margins and wetland mosaics
identification: Broad head and stocky legs
Greyish coat with dark spots and head stripes
Short, muscular tail

summary: A small Asian cat with highly variable spotting and colour. Northern individuals tend to have thicker coats; this catalogue separates it from the Sunda leopard cat.
range: Mainland Asia and nearby islands including Taiwan and parts of Japan
habitat: Forests, scrub, grassland and some agricultural landscapes
identification: Small spotted body with pale underparts
Dark forehead and cheek stripes
Rounded ears with pale marks on the backs
taxonomy_note: Separated from Prionailurus javanensis in this taxonomy. Photographs alone may not reliably distinguish them.

summary: A small spotted cat of island Southeast Asia. It was formerly grouped with the mainland leopard cat and can be very similar in appearance.
range: Java, Bali, Sumatra, Borneo and parts of the Philippines
habitat: Tropical forest, scrub, forest mosaics and some plantations
identification: Yellow-brown coat with dark spots
Pale underparts and striped face
Spotted tail with darker rings near the tip
taxonomy_note: Origin and other evidence can be needed to separate this species from the mainland leopard cat.

summary: Despite its name, this long-legged cat is often associated with reeds, wetlands and scrub rather than dense rainforest.
range: Egypt, parts of the Middle East and Central, South and Southeast Asia
habitat: Wetlands, reed beds, grasslands, scrub and cultivated areas
identification: Mostly plain sandy, grey or reddish coat
Tall ears with small dark tufts
Long legs and a relatively short, ringed tail

summary: A very small southern African cat of open, dry country. Its name refers to the dark soles and undersides of its feet, rather than entirely black legs.
range: Southern Africa, principally South Africa, Namibia and Botswana
habitat: Dry grassland, open savanna and semi-desert
identification: Small body with strong dark spots
Spots merging into bands on legs and tail
Dark soles and a short black-tipped tail

summary: A desert specialist with a pale coat and broad head. Fur beneath its paws helps protect it from the extremes of hot and cold ground.
range: North Africa, the Arabian Peninsula and parts of Southwest and Central Asia
habitat: Sandy and rocky deserts with sparse vegetation
identification: Broad, flattened head and large low-set ears
Pale sandy coat
Dark cheek lines and bars on legs or tail

summary: A little-studied cat of high-elevation China. Although once called the Chinese desert cat, it is associated with grasslands and shrublands rather than true desert.
range: Eastern Qinghai–Tibet Plateau, China
habitat: Alpine meadows, highland steppe and shrubland
identification: Stocky body with dense greyish or brown fur
Small ear tufts
Bushy tail with dark rings and tip
taxonomy_note: Recognised as a species in the 2017 reference; its relationship to other wildcats has been debated.

summary: A wildcat of Africa and parts of Asia, closely related to the domestic cat. Its appearance varies across a wide range and overlaps strongly with domestic cats.
range: Africa, the Middle East and parts of Central and South Asia
habitat: Savannas, scrub, semi-deserts and open woodland
identification: Relatively long legs and light build
Variable sandy or grey coat with stripes or spots
Slim, tapering tail with a dark tip
taxonomy_note: Includes Afro-Asiatic forms under CCTF 2017. Domestic cats and hybrids cannot reliably be excluded using a photograph alone.

summary: A thick-coated forest cat of Europe and adjoining regions. It can closely resemble a domestic tabby, and hybridisation makes visual identification particularly uncertain.
range: Parts of Europe, Anatolia and the Caucasus
habitat: Forests and nearby scrub or grassland
identification: Thick grey-brown coat with dark stripes
Broad, bushy tail with a blunt dark tip
Distinct dark rings around the tail
taxonomy_note: Appearance cannot establish genetic purity or reliably distinguish all domestic–wildcat hybrids.
